# Fort Hill
Within Clemson University's campus in South Carolina sits a site with a political past: the John C. Calhoun Mansion and Library, better known as Fort Hill, stands as a National Historic Landmark. Once the home of a prominent political figure, it currently serves as a museum.

# Fort Hill
## Learn more
This residence once belonged to John C. Calhoun, the seventh Vice President of the United States, offering a peek into his life and times. Constructed in the early 19th century, it is a fine example of Greek Revival architecture. The property stayed in the Calhoun family until it was donated to Clemson University, thanks in part to Thomas Green Clemson's pivotal involvement. Inside, visitors can find original furnishings that provide a snapshot of its former occupants' daily lives. The property also has a calm landscape, though it is interwoven with the complex historical context of enslaved labor. Clemson University utilizes the site for educational outreach, emphasizing the narratives of the enslaved individuals who lived and worked on the grounds.

April 15, 2026, 7:12 a.m. ET
*   Fort Hill, located on Clemson University's campus, is the former plantation home of statesman John C. Calhoun.  
*   The property was later inherited by Thomas Green Clemson, who bequeathed it to establish the university.  
*   The site is now a public museum that explores its layered history, including its ties to slavery and politics.  
*   Fort Hill is preserved as an educational resource and is integrated into the university's curriculum.
A white-columned house stands quietly preserved on Clemson University's campus.
Fort Hill is a national historic landmark and the former home of John C. Calhoun. The home has a layered history, from its ties to politics and slavery to its role in Clemson's founding. The site now sits as a public museum.
Calhoun, the seventh vice president of the United States (1825-1832) and a U.S. senator, lived in the home at Fort Hill from 1825 until he died in 1850.
Fort Hill is also the site of the first meeting of the board of the trustees of the Clemson Agriculture College.
Clemson Agricultural College opened in July 1893 with 446 students.
Clemson became a coeducational institution in 1955.
In 1963, with the admission of Harvey Ganntt, Clemson became the first white institution in South Carolina to desegregate since Reconstruction.
The institution became Clemson University in 1964. Clemson currently has a total undergraduate enrollment of over 23,000.

## Enslaved men, women lived and worked at the plantation
According to Greenville News archives, Clemson University was founded in 1889 through a bequest from Thomas Green Clemson, a Philadelphia-born, European-educated engineer, musician and artist. He married Anna Maria, daughter of the former U.S. vice president and Sen.John C. Calhoun, according to Clemson University. The university was built on Fort Hill, and the plantation was owned by Calhoun and his wife, Floride.
The town of Calhoun was formally incorporated in 1937, but was renamed the cityof Clemson in 1943 to "eliminate confusion with Calhoun Falls and to officially recognize the 'town-gown' partnership," according to the city.
Enslaved men and women once lived on the plantation and built parts of the university campus, according to a 2019 Greenville News article.
"The piedmont frontier of South Carolina was developed into plantations by African Americans in bondage," according to theClemson University website. "Their resilience, determination, and resistance are essential to the full and complete history of the land we know as Clemson University."

## Fort Hill's significance
Fort Hill and Calhoun House are significant for their ties to John C. Calhoun and the founding of Clemson University. The home reflects Southern political and social history, including slavery, and remains central to ongoing discussions about how that history is interpreted and presented.
Fort Hill was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1975 by the National Park Service and the United States Department of the Interior.

## Things to do before/after a museum visit
While you're in Clemson, visitors can stop by the Hanson Visitor's Center, Keowee-Toxaway State Park, Devils Fork State Park, and Memorial Stadium.
Other sites around Clemson are the Bob Campbell Geology Museum and the South Carolina Botanical Gardens.
If visitors want a meal or coffee, there's All In Coffee Shop at 106 Earl St., Moe Joe Coffee and Music House at 385 Old Greenville Highway, and SunnySide Cafe at 147A Sloan St.

## Planning your visit
*   **Best time:**The best time to visit the museum is during non-semester hours, when the site isn't as busy.

*   **Hours/admission:**The Fort Hill Museum is open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to noon and 1 to 4:30 p.m., and Sunday from 2 to 4:30 p.m. The site is closed on university holidays, home football game days, and for special events, staff training, and conferences.

*   **Learn more:**Visit Clemson University'swebsite for more information about Fort Hill.

# Fort Hill property proposed to become Clemson museum
Blake Mauro, Associate Editor
November 17, 2022
Clemson News // Courtesy
The Fort Hill House is located on-campus, and will be transformed into a museum going forward.
Clemson Libraries plans to reinvent the Fort Hill property to better “tell the story of Clemson,” according to Christopher Cox, dean of Clemson Libraries, at Monday’s Student Senate meeting.
If approved, the library intends to convert the property into a Clemson museum that tells the full story of Clemson, which may not be “exactly what you expect,” according to Cox.
The facilities that currently operate within the Trustee House located on the Fort Hill property will be relocated to Daniel Hall once construction on the building is completed, according to Cox.
The library plans to transform the Trustee House into an interpretive center that will house rotating exhibits to showcase Clemson’s rich history.
Along with the physical museum, the library hopes to offer classes and creative inquiry opportunities that explore the history of the University property, as the position of University Historian is now also under the jurisdiction of the library.
The creative inquiry course will be open to open to all Clemson students and will be open for enrollment in the fall 2023 semester.
Cox acknowledged that Fort Hill itself has a mixed history with both “positive and questionable” attributes.
In 1836, the property came under the ownership of John C. Calhoun, a prominent Southern politician who owned most of the land that Clemson University sits on; it was known as the Fort Hill Plantation.
When Calhoun died in 1850, his wife Floride became the sole owner of the Fort Hill home and 1,341 acres of land.
At the time of Calhoun’s death, 75 enslaved African Americans lived and worked at Fort Hill, according to U.S. Census data.
In 1888, Clemson bequeathed three-fourths of the Fort Hill plantation and $80,000 to the state of South Carolina for the establishment of a public scientific and agricultural college.
Clemson willed that Fort Hill “shall always be open for the inspection of visitors.”
Clemson Libraries plans to carry on Thomas Green Clemson’s vision by opening the Clemson Museum for students, faculty and Clemson community members to visit, learn and explore.

Within Clemson University's campus in South Carolina sits a site with a political past: the John C. Calhoun Mansion and Library, better known as Fort Hill, stands as a National Historic Landmark. Once the home of a prominent political figure, it currently serves as a museum.
texts.2:
# Fort Hill
## Learn more
This residence once belonged to John C. Calhoun, the seventh Vice President of the United States, offering a peek into his life and times. Constructed in the early 19th century, it is a fine example of Greek Revival architecture. The property stayed in the Calhoun family until it was donated to Clemson University, thanks in part to Thomas Green Clemson's pivotal involvement. Inside, visitors can find original furnishings that provide a snapshot of its former occupants' daily lives. The property also has a calm landscape, though it is interwoven with the complex historical context of enslaved labor. Clemson University utilizes the site for educational outreach, emphasizing the narratives of the enslaved individuals who lived and worked on the grounds.

April 15, 2026, 7:12 a.m. ET
*   Fort Hill, located on Clemson University's campus, is the former plantation home of statesman John C. Calhoun.  
*   The property was later inherited by Thomas Green Clemson, who bequeathed it to establish the university.  
*   The site is now a public museum that explores its layered history, including its ties to slavery and politics.  
*   Fort Hill is preserved as an educational resource and is integrated into the university's curriculum.
A white-columned house stands quietly preserved on Clemson University's campus.
Fort Hill is a national historic landmark and the former home of John C. Calhoun. The home has a layered history, from its ties to politics and slavery to its role in Clemson's founding. The site now sits as a public museum.
Calhoun, the seventh vice president of the United States (1825-1832) and a U.S. senator, lived in the home at Fort Hill from 1825 until he died in 1850.
Fort Hill is also the site of the first meeting of the board of the trustees of the Clemson Agriculture College.
Clemson Agricultural College opened in July 1893 with 446 students.
Clemson became a coeducational institution in 1955.
In 1963, with the admission of Harvey Ganntt, Clemson became the first white institution in South Carolina to desegregate since Reconstruction.
The institution became Clemson University in 1964. Clemson currently has a total undergraduate enrollment of over 23,000.
texts.1:
## Enslaved men, women lived and worked at the plantation
According to Greenville News archives, Clemson University was founded in 1889 through a bequest from Thomas Green Clemson, a Philadelphia-born, European-educated engineer, musician and artist. He married Anna Maria, daughter of the former U.S. vice president and Sen.John C. Calhoun, according to Clemson University. The university was built on Fort Hill, and the plantation was owned by Calhoun and his wife, Floride.
The town of Calhoun was formally incorporated in 1937, but was renamed the cityof Clemson in 1943 to "eliminate confusion with Calhoun Falls and to officially recognize the 'town-gown' partnership," according to the city.
Enslaved men and women once lived on the plantation and built parts of the university campus, according to a 2019 Greenville News article.
"The piedmont frontier of South Carolina was developed into plantations by African Americans in bondage," according to theClemson University website. "Their resilience, determination, and resistance are essential to the full and complete history of the land we know as Clemson University."
texts.2:
## Fort Hill's significance
Fort Hill and Calhoun House are significant for their ties to John C. Calhoun and the founding of Clemson University. The home reflects Southern political and social history, including slavery, and remains central to ongoing discussions about how that history is interpreted and presented.
Fort Hill was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1975 by the National Park Service and the United States Department of the Interior.
texts.3:
## Things to do before/after a museum visit
While you're in Clemson, visitors can stop by the Hanson Visitor's Center, Keowee-Toxaway State Park, Devils Fork State Park, and Memorial Stadium.
Other sites around Clemson are the Bob Campbell Geology Museum and the South Carolina Botanical Gardens.
If visitors want a meal or coffee, there's All In Coffee Shop at 106 Earl St., Moe Joe Coffee and Music House at 385 Old Greenville Highway, and SunnySide Cafe at 147A Sloan St.
texts.4:
## Planning your visit
*   **Best time:**The best time to visit the museum is during non-semester hours, when the site isn't as busy.

*   **Hours/admission:**The Fort Hill Museum is open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to noon and 1 to 4:30 p.m., and Sunday from 2 to 4:30 p.m. The site is closed on university holidays, home football game days, and for special events, staff training, and conferences.

*   **Learn more:**Visit Clemson University'swebsite for more information about Fort Hill.

# Fort Hill property proposed to become Clemson museum
Blake Mauro, Associate Editor
November 17, 2022
Clemson News // Courtesy
The Fort Hill House is located on-campus, and will be transformed into a museum going forward.
Clemson Libraries plans to reinvent the Fort Hill property to better “tell the story of Clemson,” according to Christopher Cox, dean of Clemson Libraries, at Monday’s Student Senate meeting.
If approved, the library intends to convert the property into a Clemson museum that tells the full story of Clemson, which may not be “exactly what you expect,” according to Cox.
The facilities that currently operate within the Trustee House located on the Fort Hill property will be relocated to Daniel Hall once construction on the building is completed, according to Cox.
The library plans to transform the Trustee House into an interpretive center that will house rotating exhibits to showcase Clemson’s rich history.
Along with the physical museum, the library hopes to offer classes and creative inquiry opportunities that explore the history of the University property, as the position of University Historian is now also under the jurisdiction of the library.
The creative inquiry course will be open to open to all Clemson students and will be open for enrollment in the fall 2023 semester.
Cox acknowledged that Fort Hill itself has a mixed history with both “positive and questionable” attributes.
In 1836, the property came under the ownership of John C. Calhoun, a prominent Southern politician who owned most of the land that Clemson University sits on; it was known as the Fort Hill Plantation.
When Calhoun died in 1850, his wife Floride became the sole owner of the Fort Hill home and 1,341 acres of land.
At the time of Calhoun’s death, 75 enslaved African Americans lived and worked at Fort Hill, according to U.S. Census data.
In 1888, Clemson bequeathed three-fourths of the Fort Hill plantation and $80,000 to the state of South Carolina for the establishment of a public scientific and agricultural college.
Clemson willed that Fort Hill “shall always be open for the inspection of visitors.”
Clemson Libraries plans to carry on Thomas Green Clemson’s vision by opening the Clemson Museum for students, faculty and Clemson community members to visit, learn and explore.

Within Clemson University's campus in South Carolina sits a site with a political past: the John C. Calhoun Mansion and Library, better known as Fort Hill, stands as a National Historic Landmark. Once the home of a prominent political figure, it currently serves as a museum.

# Fort Hill
## Learn more
This residence once belonged to John C. Calhoun, the seventh Vice President of the United States, offering a peek into his life and times. Constructed in the early 19th century, it is a fine example of Greek Revival architecture. The property stayed in the Calhoun family until it was donated to Clemson University, thanks in part to Thomas Green Clemson's pivotal involvement. Inside, visitors can find original furnishings that provide a snapshot of its former occupants' daily lives. The property also has a calm landscape, though it is interwoven with the complex historical context of enslaved labor. Clemson University utilizes the site for educational outreach, emphasizing the narratives of the enslaved individuals who lived and worked on the grounds.

Title: America 250: How to visit historic home at Clemson University

April 15, 2026, 7:12 a.m. ET
*   Fort Hill, located on Clemson University's campus, is the former plantation home of statesman John C. Calhoun.  
*   The property was later inherited by Thomas Green Clemson, who bequeathed it to establish the university.  
*   The site is now a public museum that explores its layered history, including its ties to slavery and politics.  
*   Fort Hill is preserved as an educational resource and is integrated into the university's curriculum.
A white-columned house stands quietly preserved on Clemson University's campus.
Fort Hill is a national historic landmark and the former home of John C. Calhoun. The home has a layered history, from its ties to politics and slavery to its role in Clemson's founding. The site now sits as a public museum.
Calhoun, the seventh vice president of the United States (1825-1832) and a U.S. senator, lived in the home at Fort Hill from 1825 until he died in 1850.
Fort Hill is also the site of the first meeting of the board of the trustees of the Clemson Agriculture College.
Clemson Agricultural College opened in July 1893 with 446 students.
Clemson became a coeducational institution in 1955.
In 1963, with the admission of Harvey Ganntt, Clemson became the first white institution in South Carolina to desegregate since Reconstruction.
The institution became Clemson University in 1964. Clemson currently has a total undergraduate enrollment of over 23,000.

## Enslaved men, women lived and worked at the plantation
According to Greenville News archives, Clemson University was founded in 1889 through a bequest from Thomas Green Clemson, a Philadelphia-born, European-educated engineer, musician and artist. He married Anna Maria, daughter of the former U.S. vice president and Sen.John C. Calhoun, according to Clemson University. The university was built on Fort Hill, and the plantation was owned by Calhoun and his wife, Floride.
The town of Calhoun was formally incorporated in 1937, but was renamed the cityof Clemson in 1943 to "eliminate confusion with Calhoun Falls and to officially recognize the 'town-gown' partnership," according to the city.
Enslaved men and women once lived on the plantation and built parts of the university campus, according to a 2019 Greenville News article.
"The piedmont frontier of South Carolina was developed into plantations by African Americans in bondage," according to theClemson University website. "Their resilience, determination, and resistance are essential to the full and complete history of the land we know as Clemson University."

## Fort Hill's significance
Fort Hill and Calhoun House are significant for their ties to John C. Calhoun and the founding of Clemson University. The home reflects Southern political and social history, including slavery, and remains central to ongoing discussions about how that history is interpreted and presented.
Fort Hill was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1975 by the National Park Service and the United States Department of the Interior.

## Things to do before/after a museum visit
While you're in Clemson, visitors can stop by the Hanson Visitor's Center, Keowee-Toxaway State Park, Devils Fork State Park, and Memorial Stadium.
Other sites around Clemson are the Bob Campbell Geology Museum and the South Carolina Botanical Gardens.
If visitors want a meal or coffee, there's All In Coffee Shop at 106 Earl St., Moe Joe Coffee and Music House at 385 Old Greenville Highway, and SunnySide Cafe at 147A Sloan St.

## Planning your visit
*   **Best time:**The best time to visit the museum is during non-semester hours, when the site isn't as busy.

*   **Hours/admission:**The Fort Hill Museum is open Monday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to noon and 1 to 4:30 p.m., and Sunday from 2 to 4:30 p.m. The site is closed on university holidays, home football game days, and for special events, staff training, and conferences.

*   **Learn more:**Visit Clemson University'swebsite for more information about Fort Hill.

# Fort Hill property proposed to become Clemson museum
Blake Mauro, Associate Editor
November 17, 2022
Clemson News // Courtesy
The Fort Hill House is located on-campus, and will be transformed into a museum going forward.
Clemson Libraries plans to reinvent the Fort Hill property to better “tell the story of Clemson,” according to Christopher Cox, dean of Clemson Libraries, at Monday’s Student Senate meeting.
If approved, the library intends to convert the property into a Clemson museum that tells the full story of Clemson, which may not be “exactly what you expect,” according to Cox.
The facilities that currently operate within the Trustee House located on the Fort Hill property will be relocated to Daniel Hall once construction on the building is completed, according to Cox.
The library plans to transform the Trustee House into an interpretive center that will house rotating exhibits to showcase Clemson’s rich history.
Along with the physical museum, the library hopes to offer classes and creative inquiry opportunities that explore the history of the University property, as the position of University Historian is now also under the jurisdiction of the library.
The creative inquiry course will be open to open to all Clemson students and will be open for enrollment in the fall 2023 semester.
Cox acknowledged that Fort Hill itself has a mixed history with both “positive and questionable” attributes.
In 1836, the property came under the ownership of John C. Calhoun, a prominent Southern politician who owned most of the land that Clemson University sits on; it was known as the Fort Hill Plantation.
When Calhoun died in 1850, his wife Floride became the sole owner of the Fort Hill home and 1,341 acres of land.
At the time of Calhoun’s death, 75 enslaved African Americans lived and worked at Fort Hill, according to U.S. Census data.
In 1888, Clemson bequeathed three-fourths of the Fort Hill plantation and $80,000 to the state of South Carolina for the establishment of a public scientific and agricultural college.
Clemson willed that Fort Hill “shall always be open for the inspection of visitors.”
Clemson Libraries plans to carry on Thomas Green Clemson’s vision by opening the Clemson Museum for students, faculty and Clemson community members to visit, learn and explore.

The University Relations office clarified that the project will need to go through the appropriate building approvals before action is taken, and the article has been updated with this information._

**WSFN** (790 AM) is a commercial radio station licensed to Brunswick, Georgia, United States, and serving Coastal Georgia and the Golden Isles with a sports radio format. Programming is simulcast on WFNS1350 AM and on FM translator**W279BC** at 103.7 MHz. Southern Media Interactive LLC owns WSFN and also WSEG in Savannah and WFNS in Blackshear. Most of the programming comes from ESPN Radio. The station also carries Atlanta Bravesbaseball games.
The station first signed on the air on September 1, 1966.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-2) It went through multiple formats over the years. In 1998, it switched to all sports radio programming. "The Fan" SportsRadio 790 WSFN was the first and only full-time, 24-hour all-sports radio station serving Brunswick and The Golden Isles of Georgia, brought here by MarMac Communications, LLC., along with WFNS, WSEG, Savannah.
In March 2013, Southern Media Interactive, LLC, acquired WSFN, WFNS and WSEG. The company created the Southern Pigskin Radio Network, broadcasting on all five AM/FM stations in the Brunswick, Savannah and Hilton Head radio markets.

The station is an affiliate of the Atlanta Braves Radio Network, the largest radio network in Major League Baseball.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-3) Regular programming on WSFN is pre-empted when the Braves are playing.
On September 4, 2022, it was announced that Shanks Broadcasting would acquire WSFN and would begin carrying the company's "Sports Superstations" network.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-4)
In March 2024, WSFN was told by the Federal Communications Commission that it would be fined $16,200 and would lose the license to run its FM translator at 103.7 MHz. The FCC said WSFN had committed numerous violations, including being off the air without notifying the FCC, operating from a location not on its license and using equipment not on its license.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-5) WSFN management is considering contesting the fine and translator revocation.

**WSFN** (790 AM) is a commercial radio station licensed to Brunswick, Georgia, United States, and serving Coastal Georgia and the Golden Isles with a sports radio format. Programming is simulcast on WFNS1350 AM and on FM translator**W279BC** at 103.7 MHz. Southern Media Interactive LLC owns WSFN and also WSEG in Savannah and WFNS in Blackshear. Most of the programming comes from ESPN Radio. The station also carries Atlanta Bravesbaseball games.
The station first signed on the air on September 1, 1966.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-2) It went through multiple formats over the years. In 1998, it switched to all sports radio programming. "The Fan" SportsRadio 790 WSFN was the first and only full-time, 24-hour all-sports radio station serving Brunswick and The Golden Isles of Georgia, brought here by MarMac Communications, LLC., along with WFNS, WSEG, Savannah.
In March 2013, Southern Media Interactive, LLC, acquired WSFN, WFNS and WSEG. The company created the Southern Pigskin Radio Network, broadcasting on all five AM/FM stations in the Brunswick, Savannah and Hilton Head radio markets.

The station is an affiliate of the Atlanta Braves Radio Network, the largest radio network in Major League Baseball.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-3) Regular programming on WSFN is pre-empted when the Braves are playing.
On September 4, 2022, it was announced that Shanks Broadcasting would acquire WSFN and would begin carrying the company's "Sports Superstations" network.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-4)
In March 2024, WSFN was told by the Federal Communications Commission that it would be fined $16,200 and would lose the license to run its FM translator at 103.7 MHz. The FCC said WSFN had committed numerous violations, including being off the air without notifying the FCC, operating from a location not on its license and using equipment not on its license.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-5) WSFN management is considering contesting the fine and translator revocation.

**WSFN** (790 AM) is a commercial radio station licensed to Brunswick, Georgia, United States, and serving Coastal Georgia and the Golden Isles with a sports radio format. Programming is simulcast on WFNS1350 AM and on FM translator**W279BC** at 103.7 MHz. Southern Media Interactive LLC owns WSFN and also WSEG in Savannah and WFNS in Blackshear. Most of the programming comes from ESPN Radio. The station also carries Atlanta Bravesbaseball games.
The station first signed on the air on September 1, 1966.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-2) It went through multiple formats over the years. In 1998, it switched to all sports radio programming. "The Fan" SportsRadio 790 WSFN was the first and only full-time, 24-hour all-sports radio station serving Brunswick and The Golden Isles of Georgia, brought here by MarMac Communications, LLC., along with WFNS, WSEG, Savannah.
In March 2013, Southern Media Interactive, LLC, acquired WSFN, WFNS and WSEG. The company created the Southern Pigskin Radio Network, broadcasting on all five AM/FM stations in the Brunswick, Savannah and Hilton Head radio markets.

The station is an affiliate of the Atlanta Braves Radio Network, the largest radio network in Major League Baseball.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-3) Regular programming on WSFN is pre-empted when the Braves are playing.
On September 4, 2022, it was announced that Shanks Broadcasting would acquire WSFN and would begin carrying the company's "Sports Superstations" network.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-4)
In March 2024, WSFN was told by the Federal Communications Commission that it would be fined $16,200 and would lose the license to run its FM translator at 103.7 MHz. The FCC said WSFN had committed numerous violations, including being off the air without notifying the FCC, operating from a location not on its license and using equipment not on its license.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WSFN#cite_note-5) WSFN management is considering contesting the fine and translator revocation.

## Political career
### Senate tenure
Edwards served on the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, the U.S. Senate Committee on Judiciary, and was a member of the New Democrat Coalition._[citation needed_]
Before the 2004 Senate election, Edwards announced his retirement from the Senate and supported Erskine Bowles, former White House Chief of Staff, as the successor to his seat; Bowles was defeated by Republican Richard Burr in the election._[citation needed_]

## Political career
### Post-Senate activities
Susan Sarandon and Tim Robbins appear alongside Edwards at a presidential campaign rally in 2008
The day after his concession speech, he announced his wife Elizabeth had been diagnosed with breast cancer. Edwards told interviewer Larry King that he doubted he would return to practice as a trial lawyer and showed no interest in succeeding Terry McAuliffe as the Democratic National Committee chairman.
In February 2005, Edwards headlined the "100 Club" Dinner, a major fundraiser for the New Hampshire Democratic Party. That same month, Edwards was appointed as director of the Center on Poverty, Work and Opportunity at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill for studying ways to move people out of poverty. That fall, Edwards toured ten major universities in order to promote "Opportunity Rocks!", a program aimed at getting youth involved to fight poverty.
On March 21, 2005, Edwards recorded his first podcast[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-Podcast-38) with his wife. Several months later, in August, Edwards delivered an address to a potential key supporter in the Iowa caucus, the AFL–CIO in Waterloo, Iowa.
In the following month, Edwards sent an email to his supporters and announced that he opposed the nomination of Judge John G. Roberts to become Chief Justice of the United States. He was also opposed to the nomination of Justice Samuel Alito as an Associate Justice and Judge Charles Pickering's appointment to the Federal bench.
During the summer and fall of 2005, he visited homeless shelters and job training centers and spoke at events organized by ACORN, the NAACP and the SEIU. He spoke in favor of an expansion of the earned income tax credit; in favor of a crackdown on predatory lending; an increase in the capital gains tax rate; housing vouchers for racial minorities (to integrate upper-income neighborhoods); and a program modeled on the Works Progress Administration to rehabilitate the Gulf Coast following Hurricane Katrina. In Greene County, North Carolina, he unveiled the pilot program for College for Everyone, an educational measure he promised during his presidential campaign, in which prospective college students would receive a scholarship for their first year in exchange for ten hours of work a week. The College for Everyone program was canceled in July 2008.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-39)

## Political career
### Post-Senate activities
Edwards was co-chair of a Council on Foreign Relations task force on United States-Russia relations alongside Republican Jack Kemp, a former congressman, Cabinet official and vice presidential nominee.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-40) The task force issued its report in March 2006.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-41) On July 12, the _International Herald Tribune_ published a related op-ed by Edwards and Kemp.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-42)

## Political career
### Post-Senate activities
In October 2005, Edwards joined the Wall Street investment firm Fortress Investment Group as a senior adviser and consultant, a position for which a close aide reported he received an annual salary of $500,000.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-44) Fortress owned a major stake in Green Tree Servicing LLC, which rose to prominence in the 1990s selling subprime loans to mobile-home owners and now services subprime loans originated by others, but in an interview Edwards said he was unaware of this.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-Fortress-45) Subprime loans allow buyers with poor credit histories to be funded, but they charge higher rates because of the risk, and sometimes carry hidden fees and increased charges over time.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-Fortress-45) In August 2007, _The Wall Street Journal_ reported that a portion of the Edwards family's assets were invested in Fortress Investment Group, which had, in turn, invested a portion of its assets in subprime mortgage lenders, some of which had foreclosed on the homes of Hurricane Katrina victims.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-47) Upon learning of Fortress's investments, Edwards divested funds and stated that he would try to help the affected families.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-48) Edwards later helped set up an ACORN-administered "Louisiana Home Rescue Fund" seeded with $100,000, much of it from his pocket, to provide loans and grants to the families who were foreclosed on by Fortress-owned lenders.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-49)

## Political career
### Post-Senate activities
As of 2014, Edwards was a personal injury lawyer in Pitt County, North Carolina.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-Pitt-50) He was invited to and attended the 2024 Democratic National Convention, which was the first DNC he attended since his Vice-Presidential nomination in Boston, twenty years earlier.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-51)

## Political campaigns
### 2004 presidential campaign
In 2000, Edwards unofficially began his presidential campaign when he began to seek speaking engagements in Iowa, the site of the nation's first party caucuses. On January 2, 2003, Edwards began fundraising without officially campaigning by forming an exploratory committee. On September 15, 2003, Edwards fulfilled a promise he made a year earlier as a guest on _The Daily Show with Jon Stewart_ to unofficially announce his intention to seek the 2004 Democratic presidential nomination. The next morning, Edwards made the announcement officially from his hometown. He declined to run for reelection to the Senate in order to focus on his presidential run. Edwards's campaign was chaired by North Carolina Democratic activist Ed Turlington.
As Edwards had been building support essentially since his election to the Senate, he led the initial campaign fundraising, amassing over $7 million during the first quarter of 2003 – more than half of which came from individuals associated with the legal profession, particularly Edwards's fellow trial lawyers, their families, and employees.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-56) Edwards's stump speech spoke of "Two Americas", with one composed of the wealthy and privileged, and the other of the hard-working common man, causing the media to often characterize Edwards as a populist.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-58)

## Political campaigns
### 2004 presidential campaign
Edwards struggled to gain substantial support, but his poll numbers began to rise steadily weeks before the Iowa caucuses. In these he had a surprising second-place finish with the support of 32% of delegates, behind only John Kerry's 39% and ahead of former front-runner Howard Dean at 18%. One week later in the New Hampshire primary, Edwards finished in fourth place behind Kerry, Dean and Wesley Clark, with 12%. During the February 3 primaries, Edwards won the South Carolina primary,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-59) lost to Clark in Oklahoma, and lost to Kerry in the other states. Edwards garnered the second-largest number of second-place finishes, again falling behind Clark.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-60)
Edwards speaking at Nashua, New Hampshire, November 7th 2003
Dean withdrew from the contest, leaving Edwards the only major challenger to Kerry. In the Wisconsin primary on February 17, Edwards finished second to Kerry with 34% of the vote. He largely avoided attacking Kerry until a February 29, 2004, debate in New York, in which he characterized him as a "Washington insider" and mocked Kerry's plan to form a committee to examine trade agreements.
In the Super Tuesday primaries on March 2, Kerry finished well ahead in nine of the ten states voting, and Edwards's campaign ended. In Georgia, Edwards finished only slightly behind Kerry but, failing to win a single state, chose to withdraw from the race. He announced his official withdrawal at a press conference in Raleigh, North Carolina, on March 3. Edwards's withdrawal made major media outlets relatively early on the evening of Super Tuesday, at about 6:30 pm CST, before polls had closed in California and before caucuses in Minnesota had even begun. It is thought that the withdrawal influenced many people in Minnesota to vote for other candidates, which may partially account for the strong Minnesota finish of Dennis Kucinich._[original research?_] Edwards did win the presidential straw poll conducted by the Independence Party of Minnesota.

## Political campaigns
### 2004 presidential campaign
After withdrawing from the race, he went on to win the April 17 Democratic caucuses in his home state of North Carolina,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-61) making him the only Democratic candidate besides Kerry to win nominating contests in two states in 2004.

## Political campaigns
### 2004 vice presidential nomination
On July 6, 2004, Kerry announced that Edwards would be his running mate; the decision was widely hailed in public opinion polls and by Democratic leaders. Though many Democrats supported Edwards's nomination, others criticized the selection for Edwards's perceived lack of experience. In the vice presidential debate, Dick Cheney told Edwards they had never met because of Edwards's frequent absences from the Senate, but that was later proven to be incorrect. Videotape later surfaced of Cheney and Edwards shaking hands off-camera during a taping of _Meet the Press_ on April 8, 2001.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-62) On February 1, 2001, Cheney thanked Edwards by name and sat with him during a Senate prayer breakfast. George W. Bush's campaign spokesman Steve Schmidt described the event as an "inconsequential meeting".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-64) On January 8, 2003, they met when John Edwards accompanied then-Senator Elizabeth Dole to her swearing-in while Cheney was President of the Senate.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-65)
Kerry's campaign advisor Bob Shrum later reported in _Time_ magazine that Kerry said he wished he had never picked Edwards, and the two have since stopped speaking to each other.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-66) Edwards said in his concession speech, "You can be disappointed, but you cannot walk away. This fight has just begun."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-67)

## Political campaigns
### 2008 presidential campaign
John Edwards campaigning in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania on Labor Day in 2007
On December 28, 2006, John Edwards officially announced his candidacy for President in the 2008 election from the yard of a home in New Orleans, Louisiana, that was being rebuilt after Hurricane Katrina destroyed it.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-69) Edwards stated that his main goals were eliminating poverty, fighting global warming, providing universal health care, and withdrawing troops from Iraq.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-70)
National polls had Edwards placing third among the Democratic field beginning in January 2007, behind Senator Hillary Clinton and Senator Barack Obama.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-71) By July 2007, the Edwards campaign had raised $23 million from nearly 100,000 donors, placing him behind Obama and Clinton in fundraising.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-72)
Edwards was first to boycott a Fox News-sponsored presidential debate in March 2007.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-73) Hillary Clinton, Bill Richardson, and Barack Obama followed suit.

## Background and announcement
Edwards' stump speech centered on the theme of "two Americas", contrasting the economic and political opportunities available to wealthy and powerful Americans with those available to working and middle-class families.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-29) The theme, together with Edwards' emphasis on fairness, jobs and economic opportunity, led news coverage to characterize his campaign as a form of southern or economic populism.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-30) Edwards also made his refusal to engage in sustained personal attacks on Democratic opponents part of his campaign style, describing his message as positive and "uplifting".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-32)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
[edit]
Edwards struggled to gain substantial support for much of 2003, but his poll numbers rose sharply in the final weeks before the Iowa caucuses. As recently as November he had been polling in single digits there, and his late momentum was aided by the endorsement of _The Des Moines Register_ and growing crowds at campaign events.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-33) Edwards finished a surprising second in Iowa with 32 percent of state delegate equivalents, behind Kerry's 38 percent and ahead of former front-runner Howard Dean at 18 percent.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-35) One week later in the New Hampshire primary, he finished fourth behind Kerry, Dean and Wesley Clark, with about 12 percent of the vote.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-37)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
During the February 3 contests, Edwards won the South Carolina primary with about 45 percent of the vote, his first statewide victory.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-39) In Oklahoma, he finished narrowly behind Clark, while Kerry won Arizona, Delaware, Missouri, New Mexico and North Dakota.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-41) Kerry then won the February 7 caucuses in Michigan and Washington; Edwards finished third in Michigan and fourth in Washington, having focused more heavily on the approaching contests in the South.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-43)
Edwards subsequently finished second to Kerry in Tennessee and Virginia. In Wisconsin on February 17, he again finished second, receiving about 34 percent to Kerry's 40 percent and Dean's 18 percent.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-45) Dean ended his active campaign the following day, leaving Edwards as Kerry's only remaining major challenger and turning the contest into a two-man race ahead of the ten-state March 2 round.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-47)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
Edwards largely avoided directly attacking Kerry until the final days before Super Tuesday. At a February 26 debate in Los Angeles, he emphasized their differences on trade, special interests and electability and argued that Kerry was too closely identified with Washington.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-48) In the February 29 New York debate, their sharpest exchange of the primary campaign, Edwards explicitly portrayed Kerry as a "Washington insider" and mocked Kerry's proposal for a 120-day review of trade agreements as a "Washington committee" response to families that had lost jobs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-50)
In the Super Tuesday primaries and caucuses on March 2, Kerry won nine of the ten states voting; the only exception was Vermont, won by the withdrawn Dean.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-52) Edwards came closest in Georgia but failed to win a state and decided to end his campaign. Reports of his impending withdrawal circulated during the evening of March 2, before voting or caucusing had concluded everywhere; he formally suspended his campaign in Raleigh the following day and endorsed Kerry.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-54)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
Because reports of Edwards' impending withdrawal reached Minnesota as the state's caucuses were beginning, it has been suggested that the timing influenced some caucus-goers and may have contributed to the comparatively strong finish of Dennis Kucinich._[citation needed_] Minnesota Public Radio reported that Kerry ultimately received just over half of the preference vote, Edwards 27 percent and Kucinich 17 percent.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-55) Edwards also won a presidential straw poll conducted by the Independence Party of Minnesota._[citation needed_]
Key results are shown below. The percentages are rounded to whole numbers. State-administered primary results are cross-checked against the Federal Election Commission's official 2004 compilation; caucus placements and rounded figures are also reflected in contemporaneous national and regional reporting.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-56)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-58)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-59)

## Political career
### Senate tenure
Edwards served on the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, the U.S. Senate Committee on Judiciary, and was a member of the New Democrat Coalition._[citation needed_]
Before the 2004 Senate election, Edwards announced his retirement from the Senate and supported Erskine Bowles, former White House Chief of Staff, as the successor to his seat; Bowles was defeated by Republican Richard Burr in the election._[citation needed_]

## Political career
### Post-Senate activities
Susan Sarandon and Tim Robbins appear alongside Edwards at a presidential campaign rally in 2008
The day after his concession speech, he announced his wife Elizabeth had been diagnosed with breast cancer. Edwards told interviewer Larry King that he doubted he would return to practice as a trial lawyer and showed no interest in succeeding Terry McAuliffe as the Democratic National Committee chairman.
In February 2005, Edwards headlined the "100 Club" Dinner, a major fundraiser for the New Hampshire Democratic Party. That same month, Edwards was appointed as director of the Center on Poverty, Work and Opportunity at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill for studying ways to move people out of poverty. That fall, Edwards toured ten major universities in order to promote "Opportunity Rocks!", a program aimed at getting youth involved to fight poverty.
On March 21, 2005, Edwards recorded his first podcast[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-Podcast-38) with his wife. Several months later, in August, Edwards delivered an address to a potential key supporter in the Iowa caucus, the AFL–CIO in Waterloo, Iowa.
In the following month, Edwards sent an email to his supporters and announced that he opposed the nomination of Judge John G. Roberts to become Chief Justice of the United States. He was also opposed to the nomination of Justice Samuel Alito as an Associate Justice and Judge Charles Pickering's appointment to the Federal bench.
During the summer and fall of 2005, he visited homeless shelters and job training centers and spoke at events organized by ACORN, the NAACP and the SEIU. He spoke in favor of an expansion of the earned income tax credit; in favor of a crackdown on predatory lending; an increase in the capital gains tax rate; housing vouchers for racial minorities (to integrate upper-income neighborhoods); and a program modeled on the Works Progress Administration to rehabilitate the Gulf Coast following Hurricane Katrina. In Greene County, North Carolina, he unveiled the pilot program for College for Everyone, an educational measure he promised during his presidential campaign, in which prospective college students would receive a scholarship for their first year in exchange for ten hours of work a week. The College for Everyone program was canceled in July 2008.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-39)

## Political career
### Post-Senate activities
Edwards was co-chair of a Council on Foreign Relations task force on United States-Russia relations alongside Republican Jack Kemp, a former congressman, Cabinet official and vice presidential nominee.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-40) The task force issued its report in March 2006.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-41) On July 12, the _International Herald Tribune_ published a related op-ed by Edwards and Kemp.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-42)

## Political career
### Post-Senate activities
In October 2005, Edwards joined the Wall Street investment firm Fortress Investment Group as a senior adviser and consultant, a position for which a close aide reported he received an annual salary of $500,000.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-44) Fortress owned a major stake in Green Tree Servicing LLC, which rose to prominence in the 1990s selling subprime loans to mobile-home owners and now services subprime loans originated by others, but in an interview Edwards said he was unaware of this.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-Fortress-45) Subprime loans allow buyers with poor credit histories to be funded, but they charge higher rates because of the risk, and sometimes carry hidden fees and increased charges over time.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-Fortress-45) In August 2007, _The Wall Street Journal_ reported that a portion of the Edwards family's assets were invested in Fortress Investment Group, which had, in turn, invested a portion of its assets in subprime mortgage lenders, some of which had foreclosed on the homes of Hurricane Katrina victims.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-47) Upon learning of Fortress's investments, Edwards divested funds and stated that he would try to help the affected families.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-48) Edwards later helped set up an ACORN-administered "Louisiana Home Rescue Fund" seeded with $100,000, much of it from his pocket, to provide loans and grants to the families who were foreclosed on by Fortress-owned lenders.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-49)

## Political campaigns
### 2004 presidential campaign
In 2000, Edwards unofficially began his presidential campaign when he began to seek speaking engagements in Iowa, the site of the nation's first party caucuses. On January 2, 2003, Edwards began fundraising without officially campaigning by forming an exploratory committee. On September 15, 2003, Edwards fulfilled a promise he made a year earlier as a guest on _The Daily Show with Jon Stewart_ to unofficially announce his intention to seek the 2004 Democratic presidential nomination. The next morning, Edwards made the announcement officially from his hometown. He declined to run for reelection to the Senate in order to focus on his presidential run. Edwards's campaign was chaired by North Carolina Democratic activist Ed Turlington.
As Edwards had been building support essentially since his election to the Senate, he led the initial campaign fundraising, amassing over $7 million during the first quarter of 2003 – more than half of which came from individuals associated with the legal profession, particularly Edwards's fellow trial lawyers, their families, and employees.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-56) Edwards's stump speech spoke of "Two Americas", with one composed of the wealthy and privileged, and the other of the hard-working common man, causing the media to often characterize Edwards as a populist.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-58)
texts.22:
## Political campaigns
### 2004 presidential campaign
Edwards struggled to gain substantial support, but his poll numbers began to rise steadily weeks before the Iowa caucuses. In these he had a surprising second-place finish with the support of 32% of delegates, behind only John Kerry's 39% and ahead of former front-runner Howard Dean at 18%. One week later in the New Hampshire primary, Edwards finished in fourth place behind Kerry, Dean and Wesley Clark, with 12%. During the February 3 primaries, Edwards won the South Carolina primary,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-59) lost to Clark in Oklahoma, and lost to Kerry in the other states. Edwards garnered the second-largest number of second-place finishes, again falling behind Clark.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-60)
Edwards speaking at Nashua, New Hampshire, November 7th 2003
Dean withdrew from the contest, leaving Edwards the only major challenger to Kerry. In the Wisconsin primary on February 17, Edwards finished second to Kerry with 34% of the vote. He largely avoided attacking Kerry until a February 29, 2004, debate in New York, in which he characterized him as a "Washington insider" and mocked Kerry's plan to form a committee to examine trade agreements.
In the Super Tuesday primaries on March 2, Kerry finished well ahead in nine of the ten states voting, and Edwards's campaign ended. In Georgia, Edwards finished only slightly behind Kerry but, failing to win a single state, chose to withdraw from the race. He announced his official withdrawal at a press conference in Raleigh, North Carolina, on March 3. Edwards's withdrawal made major media outlets relatively early on the evening of Super Tuesday, at about 6:30 pm CST, before polls had closed in California and before caucuses in Minnesota had even begun. It is thought that the withdrawal influenced many people in Minnesota to vote for other candidates, which may partially account for the strong Minnesota finish of Dennis Kucinich._[original research?_] Edwards did win the presidential straw poll conducted by the Independence Party of Minnesota.

## Political campaigns
### 2004 presidential campaign
After withdrawing from the race, he went on to win the April 17 Democratic caucuses in his home state of North Carolina,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-61) making him the only Democratic candidate besides Kerry to win nominating contests in two states in 2004.
texts.24:
## Political campaigns
### 2004 vice presidential nomination
On July 6, 2004, Kerry announced that Edwards would be his running mate; the decision was widely hailed in public opinion polls and by Democratic leaders. Though many Democrats supported Edwards's nomination, others criticized the selection for Edwards's perceived lack of experience. In the vice presidential debate, Dick Cheney told Edwards they had never met because of Edwards's frequent absences from the Senate, but that was later proven to be incorrect. Videotape later surfaced of Cheney and Edwards shaking hands off-camera during a taping of _Meet the Press_ on April 8, 2001.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-62) On February 1, 2001, Cheney thanked Edwards by name and sat with him during a Senate prayer breakfast. George W. Bush's campaign spokesman Steve Schmidt described the event as an "inconsequential meeting".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-64) On January 8, 2003, they met when John Edwards accompanied then-Senator Elizabeth Dole to her swearing-in while Cheney was President of the Senate.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-65)
Kerry's campaign advisor Bob Shrum later reported in _Time_ magazine that Kerry said he wished he had never picked Edwards, and the two have since stopped speaking to each other.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-66) Edwards said in his concession speech, "You can be disappointed, but you cannot walk away. This fight has just begun."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-67)

## Political campaigns
### 2008 presidential campaign
John Edwards campaigning in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania on Labor Day in 2007
On December 28, 2006, John Edwards officially announced his candidacy for President in the 2008 election from the yard of a home in New Orleans, Louisiana, that was being rebuilt after Hurricane Katrina destroyed it.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-69) Edwards stated that his main goals were eliminating poverty, fighting global warming, providing universal health care, and withdrawing troops from Iraq.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-70)
National polls had Edwards placing third among the Democratic field beginning in January 2007, behind Senator Hillary Clinton and Senator Barack Obama.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-71) By July 2007, the Edwards campaign had raised $23 million from nearly 100,000 donors, placing him behind Obama and Clinton in fundraising.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-72)
Edwards was first to boycott a Fox News-sponsored presidential debate in March 2007.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-73) Hillary Clinton, Bill Richardson, and Barack Obama followed suit.
John Edwards with Bonnie Raitt, Jackson Browne, and Peter Coyote at a campaign event in Manchester, New Hampshire

## Background and announcement
Edwards' stump speech centered on the theme of "two Americas", contrasting the economic and political opportunities available to wealthy and powerful Americans with those available to working and middle-class families.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-29) The theme, together with Edwards' emphasis on fairness, jobs and economic opportunity, led news coverage to characterize his campaign as a form of southern or economic populism.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-30) Edwards also made his refusal to engage in sustained personal attacks on Democratic opponents part of his campaign style, describing his message as positive and "uplifting".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-32)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
[edit]
Edwards struggled to gain substantial support for much of 2003, but his poll numbers rose sharply in the final weeks before the Iowa caucuses. As recently as November he had been polling in single digits there, and his late momentum was aided by the endorsement of _The Des Moines Register_ and growing crowds at campaign events.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-33) Edwards finished a surprising second in Iowa with 32 percent of state delegate equivalents, behind Kerry's 38 percent and ahead of former front-runner Howard Dean at 18 percent.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-35) One week later in the New Hampshire primary, he finished fourth behind Kerry, Dean and Wesley Clark, with about 12 percent of the vote.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-37)
texts.6:
## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
During the February 3 contests, Edwards won the South Carolina primary with about 45 percent of the vote, his first statewide victory.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-39) In Oklahoma, he finished narrowly behind Clark, while Kerry won Arizona, Delaware, Missouri, New Mexico and North Dakota.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-41) Kerry then won the February 7 caucuses in Michigan and Washington; Edwards finished third in Michigan and fourth in Washington, having focused more heavily on the approaching contests in the South.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-43)
Edwards subsequently finished second to Kerry in Tennessee and Virginia. In Wisconsin on February 17, he again finished second, receiving about 34 percent to Kerry's 40 percent and Dean's 18 percent.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-45) Dean ended his active campaign the following day, leaving Edwards as Kerry's only remaining major challenger and turning the contest into a two-man race ahead of the ten-state March 2 round.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-47)
texts.7:
## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
Edwards largely avoided directly attacking Kerry until the final days before Super Tuesday. At a February 26 debate in Los Angeles, he emphasized their differences on trade, special interests and electability and argued that Kerry was too closely identified with Washington.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-48) In the February 29 New York debate, their sharpest exchange of the primary campaign, Edwards explicitly portrayed Kerry as a "Washington insider" and mocked Kerry's proposal for a 120-day review of trade agreements as a "Washington committee" response to families that had lost jobs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-50)
In the Super Tuesday primaries and caucuses on March 2, Kerry won nine of the ten states voting; the only exception was Vermont, won by the withdrawn Dean.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-52) Edwards came closest in Georgia but failed to win a state and decided to end his campaign. Reports of his impending withdrawal circulated during the evening of March 2, before voting or caucusing had concluded everywhere; he formally suspended his campaign in Raleigh the following day and endorsed Kerry.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-54)

## Political career
### Senate tenure
Edwards served on the U.S. Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, the U.S. Senate Committee on Judiciary, and was a member of the New Democrat Coalition._[citation needed_]
Before the 2004 Senate election, Edwards announced his retirement from the Senate and supported Erskine Bowles, former White House Chief of Staff, as the successor to his seat; Bowles was defeated by Republican Richard Burr in the election._[citation needed_]

## Political career
### Post-Senate activities
Susan Sarandon and Tim Robbins appear alongside Edwards at a presidential campaign rally in 2008
The day after his concession speech, he announced his wife Elizabeth had been diagnosed with breast cancer. Edwards told interviewer Larry King that he doubted he would return to practice as a trial lawyer and showed no interest in succeeding Terry McAuliffe as the Democratic National Committee chairman.
In February 2005, Edwards headlined the "100 Club" Dinner, a major fundraiser for the New Hampshire Democratic Party. That same month, Edwards was appointed as director of the Center on Poverty, Work and Opportunity at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill for studying ways to move people out of poverty. That fall, Edwards toured ten major universities in order to promote "Opportunity Rocks!", a program aimed at getting youth involved to fight poverty.
On March 21, 2005, Edwards recorded his first podcast[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-Podcast-38) with his wife. Several months later, in August, Edwards delivered an address to a potential key supporter in the Iowa caucus, the AFL–CIO in Waterloo, Iowa.
In the following month, Edwards sent an email to his supporters and announced that he opposed the nomination of Judge John G. Roberts to become Chief Justice of the United States. He was also opposed to the nomination of Justice Samuel Alito as an Associate Justice and Judge Charles Pickering's appointment to the Federal bench.
During the summer and fall of 2005, he visited homeless shelters and job training centers and spoke at events organized by ACORN, the NAACP and the SEIU. He spoke in favor of an expansion of the earned income tax credit; in favor of a crackdown on predatory lending; an increase in the capital gains tax rate; housing vouchers for racial minorities (to integrate upper-income neighborhoods); and a program modeled on the Works Progress Administration to rehabilitate the Gulf Coast following Hurricane Katrina. In Greene County, North Carolina, he unveiled the pilot program for College for Everyone, an educational measure he promised during his presidential campaign, in which prospective college students would receive a scholarship for their first year in exchange for ten hours of work a week. The College for Everyone program was canceled in July 2008.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-39)

## Political career
### Post-Senate activities
Edwards was co-chair of a Council on Foreign Relations task force on United States-Russia relations alongside Republican Jack Kemp, a former congressman, Cabinet official and vice presidential nominee.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-40) The task force issued its report in March 2006.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-41) On July 12, the _International Herald Tribune_ published a related op-ed by Edwards and Kemp.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-42)

## Political career
### Post-Senate activities
In October 2005, Edwards joined the Wall Street investment firm Fortress Investment Group as a senior adviser and consultant, a position for which a close aide reported he received an annual salary of $500,000.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-43)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-44) Fortress owned a major stake in Green Tree Servicing LLC, which rose to prominence in the 1990s selling subprime loans to mobile-home owners and now services subprime loans originated by others, but in an interview Edwards said he was unaware of this.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-Fortress-45) Subprime loans allow buyers with poor credit histories to be funded, but they charge higher rates because of the risk, and sometimes carry hidden fees and increased charges over time.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-Fortress-45) In August 2007, _The Wall Street Journal_ reported that a portion of the Edwards family's assets were invested in Fortress Investment Group, which had, in turn, invested a portion of its assets in subprime mortgage lenders, some of which had foreclosed on the homes of Hurricane Katrina victims.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-47) Upon learning of Fortress's investments, Edwards divested funds and stated that he would try to help the affected families.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-48) Edwards later helped set up an ACORN-administered "Louisiana Home Rescue Fund" seeded with $100,000, much of it from his pocket, to provide loans and grants to the families who were foreclosed on by Fortress-owned lenders.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-49)

## Political career
### Post-Senate activities
As of 2014, Edwards was a personal injury lawyer in Pitt County, North Carolina.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-Pitt-50) He was invited to and attended the 2024 Democratic National Convention, which was the first DNC he attended since his Vice-Presidential nomination in Boston, twenty years earlier.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-51)

## Political campaigns
### 2004 presidential campaign
In 2000, Edwards unofficially began his presidential campaign when he began to seek speaking engagements in Iowa, the site of the nation's first party caucuses. On January 2, 2003, Edwards began fundraising without officially campaigning by forming an exploratory committee. On September 15, 2003, Edwards fulfilled a promise he made a year earlier as a guest on _The Daily Show with Jon Stewart_ to unofficially announce his intention to seek the 2004 Democratic presidential nomination. The next morning, Edwards made the announcement officially from his hometown. He declined to run for reelection to the Senate in order to focus on his presidential run. Edwards's campaign was chaired by North Carolina Democratic activist Ed Turlington.
As Edwards had been building support essentially since his election to the Senate, he led the initial campaign fundraising, amassing over $7 million during the first quarter of 2003 – more than half of which came from individuals associated with the legal profession, particularly Edwards's fellow trial lawyers, their families, and employees.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-56) Edwards's stump speech spoke of "Two Americas", with one composed of the wealthy and privileged, and the other of the hard-working common man, causing the media to often characterize Edwards as a populist.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-57)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-58)

## Political campaigns
### 2004 presidential campaign
Edwards struggled to gain substantial support, but his poll numbers began to rise steadily weeks before the Iowa caucuses. In these he had a surprising second-place finish with the support of 32% of delegates, behind only John Kerry's 39% and ahead of former front-runner Howard Dean at 18%. One week later in the New Hampshire primary, Edwards finished in fourth place behind Kerry, Dean and Wesley Clark, with 12%. During the February 3 primaries, Edwards won the South Carolina primary,[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-59) lost to Clark in Oklahoma, and lost to Kerry in the other states. Edwards garnered the second-largest number of second-place finishes, again falling behind Clark.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-60)
Edwards speaking at Nashua, New Hampshire, November 7th 2003
Dean withdrew from the contest, leaving Edwards the only major challenger to Kerry. In the Wisconsin primary on February 17, Edwards finished second to Kerry with 34% of the vote. He largely avoided attacking Kerry until a February 29, 2004, debate in New York, in which he characterized him as a "Washington insider" and mocked Kerry's plan to form a committee to examine trade agreements.
In the Super Tuesday primaries on March 2, Kerry finished well ahead in nine of the ten states voting, and Edwards's campaign ended. In Georgia, Edwards finished only slightly behind Kerry but, failing to win a single state, chose to withdraw from the race. He announced his official withdrawal at a press conference in Raleigh, North Carolina, on March 3. Edwards's withdrawal made major media outlets relatively early on the evening of Super Tuesday, at about 6:30 pm CST, before polls had closed in California and before caucuses in Minnesota had even begun. It is thought that the withdrawal influenced many people in Minnesota to vote for other candidates, which may partially account for the strong Minnesota finish of Dennis Kucinich._[original research?_] Edwards did win the presidential straw poll conducted by the Independence Party of Minnesota.

## Political campaigns
### 2004 presidential campaign
After withdrawing from the race, he went on to win the April 17 Democratic caucuses in his home state of North Carolina,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-61) making him the only Democratic candidate besides Kerry to win nominating contests in two states in 2004.

## Political campaigns
### 2004 vice presidential nomination
On July 6, 2004, Kerry announced that Edwards would be his running mate; the decision was widely hailed in public opinion polls and by Democratic leaders. Though many Democrats supported Edwards's nomination, others criticized the selection for Edwards's perceived lack of experience. In the vice presidential debate, Dick Cheney told Edwards they had never met because of Edwards's frequent absences from the Senate, but that was later proven to be incorrect. Videotape later surfaced of Cheney and Edwards shaking hands off-camera during a taping of _Meet the Press_ on April 8, 2001.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-62) On February 1, 2001, Cheney thanked Edwards by name and sat with him during a Senate prayer breakfast. George W. Bush's campaign spokesman Steve Schmidt described the event as an "inconsequential meeting".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-63)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-64) On January 8, 2003, they met when John Edwards accompanied then-Senator Elizabeth Dole to her swearing-in while Cheney was President of the Senate.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-65)
Kerry's campaign advisor Bob Shrum later reported in _Time_ magazine that Kerry said he wished he had never picked Edwards, and the two have since stopped speaking to each other.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-66) Edwards said in his concession speech, "You can be disappointed, but you cannot walk away. This fight has just begun."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-67)

## Political campaigns
### 2008 presidential campaign
John Edwards campaigning in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania on Labor Day in 2007
On December 28, 2006, John Edwards officially announced his candidacy for President in the 2008 election from the yard of a home in New Orleans, Louisiana, that was being rebuilt after Hurricane Katrina destroyed it.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-68)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-69) Edwards stated that his main goals were eliminating poverty, fighting global warming, providing universal health care, and withdrawing troops from Iraq.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-70)
National polls had Edwards placing third among the Democratic field beginning in January 2007, behind Senator Hillary Clinton and Senator Barack Obama.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-71) By July 2007, the Edwards campaign had raised $23 million from nearly 100,000 donors, placing him behind Obama and Clinton in fundraising.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-72)
Edwards was first to boycott a Fox News-sponsored presidential debate in March 2007.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards#cite_note-73) Hillary Clinton, Bill Richardson, and Barack Obama followed suit.
John Edwards with Bonnie Raitt, Jackson Browne, and Peter Coyote at a campaign event in Manchester, New Hampshire
