## Background and announcement
Edwards' stump speech centered on the theme of "two Americas", contrasting the economic and political opportunities available to wealthy and powerful Americans with those available to working and middle-class families.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-29) The theme, together with Edwards' emphasis on fairness, jobs and economic opportunity, led news coverage to characterize his campaign as a form of southern or economic populism.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-30) Edwards also made his refusal to engage in sustained personal attacks on Democratic opponents part of his campaign style, describing his message as positive and "uplifting".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-32)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
[edit]
Edwards struggled to gain substantial support for much of 2003, but his poll numbers rose sharply in the final weeks before the Iowa caucuses. As recently as November he had been polling in single digits there, and his late momentum was aided by the endorsement of _The Des Moines Register_ and growing crowds at campaign events.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-33) Edwards finished a surprising second in Iowa with 32 percent of state delegate equivalents, behind Kerry's 38 percent and ahead of former front-runner Howard Dean at 18 percent.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-35) One week later in the New Hampshire primary, he finished fourth behind Kerry, Dean and Wesley Clark, with about 12 percent of the vote.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-37)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
During the February 3 contests, Edwards won the South Carolina primary with about 45 percent of the vote, his first statewide victory.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-39) In Oklahoma, he finished narrowly behind Clark, while Kerry won Arizona, Delaware, Missouri, New Mexico and North Dakota.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-40)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-41) Kerry then won the February 7 caucuses in Michigan and Washington; Edwards finished third in Michigan and fourth in Washington, having focused more heavily on the approaching contests in the South.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-43)
Edwards subsequently finished second to Kerry in Tennessee and Virginia. In Wisconsin on February 17, he again finished second, receiving about 34 percent to Kerry's 40 percent and Dean's 18 percent.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-44)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-45) Dean ended his active campaign the following day, leaving Edwards as Kerry's only remaining major challenger and turning the contest into a two-man race ahead of the ten-state March 2 round.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-46)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-47)

## Background and announcement
### First nominating contests
Edwards largely avoided directly attacking Kerry until the final days before Super Tuesday. At a February 26 debate in Los Angeles, he emphasized their differences on trade, special interests and electability and argued that Kerry was too closely identified with Washington.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-48) In the February 29 New York debate, their sharpest exchange of the primary campaign, Edwards explicitly portrayed Kerry as a "Washington insider" and mocked Kerry's proposal for a 120-day review of trade agreements as a "Washington committee" response to families that had lost jobs.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-50)
In the Super Tuesday primaries and caucuses on March 2, Kerry won nine of the ten states voting; the only exception was Vermont, won by the withdrawn Dean.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-51)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-52) Edwards came closest in Georgia but failed to win a state and decided to end his campaign. Reports of his impending withdrawal circulated during the evening of March 2, before voting or caucusing had concluded everywhere; he formally suspended his campaign in Raleigh the following day and endorsed Kerry.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-53)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-54)

Because reports of Edwards' impending withdrawal reached Minnesota as the state's caucuses were beginning, it has been suggested that the timing influenced some caucus-goers and may have contributed to the comparatively strong finish of Dennis Kucinich._[citation needed_] Minnesota Public Radio reported that Kerry ultimately received just over half of the preference vote, Edwards 27 percent and Kucinich 17 percent.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Edwards_2004_presidential_campaign#cite_note-55) Edwards also won a presidential straw poll conducted by the Independence Party of Minnesota._[citation needed_]

## Dalton downplays Trump’s backing of opponent in Florida House race
Bale Dalton, the Democratic nominee in Florida’s 7th Congressional District, said the president’s endorsement of Elijah, his Republican opponent, does not change his campaign strategy for the general election.
“No, it doesn’t change anything,” Dalton told MS NOW this morning. “Look, I’m not surprised that, you know, the president has endorsed Ryan Elijah because Ryan Elijah has already proved himself to be yet another rubber stamp.”
Trump endorsed Elijah earlier today after he snagged the nomination over scandal-plagued Mills, whom Trump had endorsed until his primary election loss last night.
“You know, he has said that the tariffs are working while small businesses here in Central Florida are struggling,” Dalton said of Elijah. “He has said that the economy is in a good spot. That’s certainly not anything that I’ve heard throughout these nine months of going around this district so far.”
Dalton, a Navy veteran, pointed to Elijah’s support for the war with Iran — which will hit its sixth month next week — as evidence that the Republican nominee would defect to Trump if elected to Congress.
“We’re not surprised, and frankly, not anything’s going to change in our campaign,” Dalton said. “We’re confident that we are going to win this race.”

## Jolly says he ’wholeheartedly’ rejects DSA
Jolly, the former Republican congressman turned prominent Trump critic who last night became the Democratic nominee for Florida governor, said he “wholeheartedly” rejects socialism and the Democratic Socialists of America group.
“I reject the DSA fully,wholeheartedly.I reject the DSA, and I reject socialism,” Jolly told MS NOW’s Peter Alexander in an interview moments ago.
Jolly has run a campaign intended to appeal to cross-party voters in deep red Florida, raising questions over whether he will campaign alongside Nixon, a member of the DSA who won Florida’s Democratic Senate nomination after toppling the establishment-backed Vindman.
Jolly did not directly answer when pressed on whether he would campaign with Nixon in the general election, but he called her a “fighter.”

## Nixon says she does not support defunding police
Nixon clarified today that she does not support defunding police or abolishing prisons in the wake of accusations from Moody. The incumbent has been using Nixon’s membership in the Democratic Socialists of America as fodder for attacks since the challenger secured the Democratic nomination for Florida’s Senate contest.
“No, I don’t support defunding the police,” Nixon said when asked about Moody’s criticism during an appearance on MSNOW’s “Morning Joe.” “I do support comprehensive criminal justice reform to make sure we are addressing some of the root causes of people leading into a life of crime.”
“I don’t support abolishing prisons,” Nixon said about a position of the national DSA platform. “What I do support is abolishing for-profit prisons because they exploit labor and they usher many of our children into the school-to-prison pipeline.”
Nixon’s decision to distance herself from some of the DSA’s more controversial platforms mirrors the strategy that other high-profile democratic socialist candidates have used in their campaigns.
Abdul El-Sayed, who won the Democratic nomination for Senate in Michigan, and Francesca Hong, who was a close second in Wisconsin’s Democratic gubernatorial primary, both distanced themselves on the campaign trail from their past calls to defund the police.

## Nixon credits grassroots organizing for primary win
State Rep. Angie Nixon, who won Florida’s Democratic Senate nomination in a major surprise over former National Security Council aide Alexander Vindman, credited the grassroots organizing that defined her campaign for her win.
“We knew we were going to win because we go out and talk to people and have conversations with folks,” Nixon said on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” after her win last night. “I’m a community organizer, a former union organizer, and I have been fighting for nearly two decades to address the issues that Floridians have been facing here in the state, working to increase the minimum wage to $15 an hour before I became a state lawmaker.”
Nixon’s double-digit defeat of Vindman, who was a key witness during Trump’s first impeachment trial and was backed by the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, was remarkable. The democratic socialist beat Vindman by 12 percentage points, leading him in every major metropolitan area with the exception of West Palm Beach. Nixon had been significantly outpaced in fundraising, as Vindman brought in $16 million compared with her $1 million. That means Nixon’s progressive campaign message resonated deeply with Florida voters.
“I am a union member. I recently joined the Working Families Party. I also just recently joined DSA because there were some things, the majority of things, that I’m supportive of,” Nixon said. “But just like I’m a Democrat, there are some things that I do not fully support within the Democratic Party, particularly those corporate Democrats.”

When asked by MS NOW’s Vaughn Hillyard moments ago whether both he and progressive Angie Nixon, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, can both win in Florida in November despite their policy differences, David Jolly said, “We’re going to find out.”
Speaking at his victory party in Miami, Jolly outlined the stark policy differences between him and Nixon. But he also made it clear that, ultimately, they are focused on the same issues most important to voters, and called Nixon a “fighter.”

The Republican competition to represent Florida’s safely red 6th Congressional District has been defined by the inflammatory rhetoric being traded by incumbent Rep. Randy Fine, who is Jewish, and Dan Bilzerian, a professional poker player turned influencer.
Bilzerian’s social media has featured an endless stream of luxury properties, women, fast cars and guns. But since he mounted a primary challenge against Fine, it has expanded to include antisemitic conspiracy theories and ugly antisemitic slurs.
With more than 30 million followers across various platforms, Bilzerian has called Fine a “fat Jew,” a “Jewish supremacist” and “Satan’s creepy little minion.” Bilzerian has also publicly wondered if Adolf Hitler was “a good person” and embraced explicitly antisemitic tropes, including claims that “the Jews” were responsible for the 1963 assassination of President John F. Kennedy.
Fine, on the other hand, has faced calls to resign from Congress over his anti-Muslim and anti-Palestinian statements. Trump endorsed nearly two dozen Republicans running in House races, including Catalina Lauf, his former U.S. Department of Commerce adviser who is running for the 19th District, and Rep. Randy Fine, who is running for re-election in the 6th District.
Trump previously endorsed Rep. Cory Mills, who is facing a House Ethics investigation and faces several controversies, though Mills was notably left off the president’s recent endorsement list.
In Florida’s attorney general race, Trump endorsed James Uthmeier, who was appointed to serve as attorney general to replace Moody after she filled the vacant Senate seat in February 2025.

## A free-for-all in The Last Frontier
The race to succeed term-limited Alaska Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy has become a crowded competition among 17 gubernatorial hopefuls, only four of whom will have a shot at advancing to November’s general election.
Alaska uses an open primary system that places candidates of all parties on the same ballot, with the top four vote-getters advancing to the general election regardless of party affiliation. That means the governor’s race in The Last Frontier is something of a closely contested free-for-all as the state is facing a deepening affordability and energy crisis.
On the Democratic side, former state Sen. Tom Begich, the uncle of Alaska’s at-large GOP Rep. Nick Begich, is expected to proceed to November’s general election alongside former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins. That pair will likely split Alaska’s blue votes, leaving more than a dozen of their Republican challengers to fight to win the support of the historically red state’s GOP base.
Republican businesswoman Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage Mayor Mark Bronson and former state Sen. Click Bishop have emerged as the top contenders on the Republican ticket.
With so many candidates, the difference between advancing and calling a campaign quits could come down to less than a few hundred ballots. With two candidates from each party expected to advance to November, speculation has already swirled over whether candidates will withdraw ahead of the general election to consolidate the vote.

Florida Republicans head into today’s primaries with a new congressional map designed to give the GOP a chance to expand its already dominant share of the state’s U.S. House delegation — and potentially bolster the party’s efforts to retain control of Congress.
Republicans embarked on an aggressive mid-decade redistricting push this year, taking the unusual step of redrawing congressional boundaries years before the next census. Gov. Ron DeSantis called lawmakers into a special session, and the Republican-controlled Legislature approved the new map in April. DeSantis signed it May 4.
The previous map sent 20 Republicans and eight Democrats to Congress. The new boundaries could produce as many as four additional Republican seats, potentially giving the GOP a 24-4 advantage in Florida’s 28-member House delegation.
The map puts several Democratic-held seats in significantly more difficultterritory, reshaping districts represented by Reps. Kathy Castor, Darren Soto, Jared Moskowitz and Debbie Wasserman Schultz. Today’s primaries will determine which candidates compete under those new boundaries for the first time.
Florida’s remap is part of a broader national redistricting battle ahead of November, as Republicans have pushed to redraw congressional boundaries in several GOP-controlled states in hopes of protecting their narrow House majority. Democrats have responded with redistricting efforts of their own in Democratic-led states.
The Florida map is also facing legal challengesunder the state constitution’s Fair Districts Amendment, which restricts partisan considerations in drawing congressional districts.
